extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, parents, and educators interested in reading, education, and critical study of books
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on how to choose, read, and profit from books: distinguishing ephemeral from enduring works, cultivating habits of careful attention to words, and developing the labour and sympathy required to enter into an author's thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish books of the hour vs books of all time
rubrics_metrics.description: All books are divisible into two classes, the books of the hour, and the books of all time; the distinction is one of species, not merely of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'books of the hour' (ephemeral letters, travel accounts, newspapers, lively essays) as useful or pleasant but not as substitutes for true books. Reserve deep, sustained reading and lifelong memory for 'books of all time' written for permanence. Anti-pattern: allowing transient reading to usurp the place of enduring works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand a 'Book' as written for permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: A book is written, not to multiply a voice, but to perpetuate it; the author sets down what he perceives to be true and useful so that it may remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach works intended as 'books' with the expectation of permanence and depth; value them as an author's inscription or scripture—'This is the best of me.' Contrast with texts meant merely for immediate communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read to be taught by the author (seek the author's meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Go to the author to get at his meaning, not to find your own expressed by him; ascertain his thought before judging it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppress the impulse to look for agreement. First seek the author's standpoint even when it seems strange; only afterwards judge it if you are qualified. Anti-pattern: reading to confirm preexisting opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love the authors and desire to enter into their thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: To be among the great company of past minds you must love these people and show your love by a true desire to be taught by them and to enter into their thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt humility and sympathy toward authors; accept that you may need to change your thinking. Treat the 'society of the Dead' as an open, merit-based companionship to be joined by labor and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading requires active labour—work like a miner
rubrics_metrics.description: When you come to a good book, ask yourself, 'Am I inclined to work as an Australian miner would?'—you must dig, crush, and smelt to extract the metal of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring 'pickaxes' (care, wit, learning) and a 'smelting furnace' (thoughtful soul). Expect patient, sometimes very fine, chiselling and fusing to gather even a single grain of the author's mind. Anti-pattern: passive or lazy reading expecting immediate intake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look intensely at words—read letter by letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Get into the habit of looking intensely at words, assuring yourself of their meaning, syllable by syllable—nay, letter by letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy in words is the central distinction of education; even reading ten pages of a good book with real accuracy makes you educated in some measure. Make slow, careful reading a habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know words' ancestry and etymology; hunt down suspicious words
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly every word has passed through several languages and retains deep meaning; if you do not know the Greek alphabet, learn it, and get good dictionaries to trace a word's meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When doubtful about a word, investigate its linguistic history and shifts of sense. Read Max Müller's lectures; treat etymology as a tool to understand a good writer's intended sense. Anti-pattern: casual reliance on modern sense without historical awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware 'masked words' and equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are masked words which nobody understands but which everybody uses, and for which people will fight or die, fancying they mean something definite while they are chameleons of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch words for equivocation; prefer meaning over sonorous form. Recognize political, religious, or rhetorical terms that cloak ambiguous or shifting senses. Anti-pattern: uncritical use of lofty-sounding terms to give false weight to arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer meaning over form—watch meanings more closely than accent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is right that a false Latin quantity should excite a smile, but wrong that a false English meaning should not excite a frown; let the accent of words be watched, and their meaning watched more closely still.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold writers (and speakers) accountable for precise meaning, not merely for polished phrasing. Teach and enforce semantic accuracy in discourse and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect to grasp an author's whole meaning at once
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author is worth anything, you will not get at his meaning all at once; often you will not arrive at his whole meaning for a long time—wise men hide deeper thought to reward deserving readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow readings to mature; revisit texts. Be patient with gradual comprehension and look for hidden or parabolic expression rather than immediate exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use books as a society of companionship and instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a society continually open to us—the chosen and the mighty of every place and time—assembled on our bookcase shelves; we may take fellowship and rank according to our wish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value books as conversational companions available anytime; prioritize that 'society' over fleeting social ambitions. Anti-pattern: preferring living-but-shallow social contacts over the sustained counsel of books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should be intrinsically 'advancement in life', not merely social advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents often seek education only insofar as it yields a 'position in life'; but there is an education which in itself is advancement in Life; other training may be 'advancement in Death'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for education good in itself—moral, intellectual, and enduring—rather than only instrumental training for social status. Counsel parents and students to value intrinsic over merely external rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose companions (friends) with sincerity and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion to the sincerity of our desire that our friends may be true, and our discretion in choosing them, will be the general chances of our happiness and usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same care to choosing human companions as to choosing books: prefer wise and true associates. Recognize the limits of choice but strive for discernment where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume precise word choice—each word is deliberate and necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men do not play stage tricks with words; Milton's use of 'creep, intrude, climb' are needed exhaustively—no other words would serve the turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a text, assume that apparently odd or terse wordings are purposeful; unpack why each term is used and what class of meaning it is intended to cover. Anti-pattern: dismissing bold or compressed phrasing as careless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value good ephemeral writing appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of the hour (letters, lively essays, travel accounts) are often useful and pleasant—'we ought to be entirely thankful for them'—but they are not 'books' in the full sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ephemeral writings for their proper purposes—information, entertainment, immediate utility—but do not let them replace sustained study or occupy the central role reserved for enduring works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the 'peerage of words'—distinguish noble from common words
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-educated person is learned in the peerage of words; knows words of true descent and ancient blood at a glance from modern canaille, remembering ancestry and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop sensitivity to registers, histories, and connotations of vocabulary. Train ear and eye to recognize when a word carries weight or when it is recent and colloquial; apply appropriate diction in reading and writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use linguistic tools without obsessing over full mastery of languages
rubrics_metrics.description: This does not imply trying to know Greek or Latin perfectly; it takes a whole life to learn a language, but you can ascertain the meanings through which the English word has passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ dictionaries and basic language learning (e.g., Greek alphabet) to track word senses; be pragmatic—use etymology as a reading tool rather than requiring fluency in source languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to have your motives examined—prefer duty over mere love of praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern 'advancement in life' often means desire for conspicuousness and applause; while duty and honest desire to do good should be at least secondary motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pursuing study, status, or literary aims, examine whether you act for applause or for useful/duty-driven ends. Aim to cultivate motive of service and real usefulness rather than mere vanity.
